contents.content:
If you live in Uttar Pradesh and have passed Class 12, this is one exam you should know about. The Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission (UPSSSC) holds the Combined Lower Subordinate Services exam at the Intermediate (10+2) level to fill many Group C posts in different state departments, such as Amin, Storekeeper, Supervisor, Gram Panchayat Officer and Village Development Officer.

The exam works a little differently from most others. You do not walk straight into a big written paper. First comes a screening based on your PET score, and only then the main written exam. This guide explains that flow, the pattern of the paper, the syllabus, the salary and how to prepare for it without wasting time.

The details below follow the pattern seen in recent UPSSSC notices. Age limit, fee, posts and small rules can change from one notice to the next, so check the latest advertisement at upsssc.gov.in before you apply.

First, a quick picture of the exam

Point Details
Conducted by Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission (UPSSSC)
Level Intermediate (10+2)
Type of posts Group C posts in UP government departments
Screening Shortlisting on the normalised PET score
Main exam One objective paper, 100 questions, 100 marks, 2 hours
Negative marking One-fourth (25%) of the marks of a question for each wrong answer
Interview No
After the exam Document verification

UPSSSC also runs a separate Graduate level Combined Lower Subordinate Services exam (often called Lower PCS). This page is only about the 10+2 level one.

Why PET comes before everything else

PET means Preliminary Eligibility Test. UPSSSC uses it as a common first step for most of its recruitments. You give PET once, and the score you get is then used for the posts you apply for.

Here is how it connects to this exam:

  1. You must have appeared in the PET and received a valid score. If you never gave PET, you cannot apply for this recruitment.
  2. When the post notice comes, you apply online using your PET registration number.
  3. The Commission shortlists candidates for the main exam on the basis of the normalised PET score. Candidates with a zero or negative score are not shortlisted.
  4. Shortlisted candidates give the main written exam, and the final selection is made from it.
PET marks are not just a ticket. They decide whether you reach the main exam at all, so a weak PET score can cost you the chance even if you are good in the main paper.

Which posts come under this exam?

The posts are not the same in every notice. The commission picks the posts as the departments send their requirements. In recent notices the list has included the following.

Post Extra condition seen in recent notices
Commercial Tax Collection Amin Intermediate pass
Land Acquisition Amin Intermediate pass, preference to candidates with Lekhpal training
Storekeeper and Clerk Intermediate pass
Assistant Cooperative Agriculture Supervisor Intermediate pass
Housemother Intermediate pass
Stenographer Intermediate pass
Social Welfare Supervisor Intermediate pass
Village Development Officer (Social Welfare) Intermediate pass
Gram Panchayat Officer Intermediate pass and a CCC certificate from NIELIT
Farm Clerk Intermediate pass, 3 years of experience in agricultural work and working knowledge of Hindi in Devanagari script
Sales Clerk Intermediate pass, 3 years of experience in sales work and working knowledge of Hindi in Devanagari script

Notice that a few posts ask for something more than just 12th pass, like CCC or work experience. So do not select a post in the form only because it sounds good. Read its condition first.

Eligibility, in plain points

Qualification

You need to have passed the Intermediate (10+2) exam from the UP Board or an equivalent exam. The qualification should be complete by the last date given in the notice. Graduates can apply for these posts too, since 12th is the minimum, but check the notice to see how it treats higher qualifications.

Age limit

For most posts, recent notices have set the age at 18 to 40 years, counted as on a date given in the notice. Posts that need experience, like Farm Clerk and Sales Clerk, have had a tighter range of 21 to 30 years. Relaxation in the upper limit is given to reserved categories and some other groups as per UP government rules.

  • SC, ST and other notified categories get relaxation as per state rules
  • State government employees have got a 5 year relaxation in recent notices
  • Ex-servicemen and outstanding sportspersons get relaxation under their own UP rules

Who gets the reservation

Reservation benefits are given only to the permanent residents of Uttar Pradesh. Candidates of other states are treated as Unreserved. EWS candidates need a valid EWS certificate of the financial year mentioned in the notice. For women candidates, the caste certificate made from the father’s side is accepted.

Date of birth

The date of birth written in your High School (Class 10) certificate is treated as final. If your PET form or any other record has a different date, fix that before you apply.

Application fee

The fee for the online application is very low. In recent notices it has been ₹25 for all categories, and correction of the form was free. Candidates who are shortlisted for the main exam pay a separate exam fee before they download the admit card.

The main exam: how the 100 marks are divided

The paper is a single objective paper of 100 questions and 100 marks, with 2 hours to solve it. Every question carries 1 mark. The paper has three parts, and the table below shows how the marks are spread.

Part Subject Questions Marks
Part 1 History of India and Indian National Movement 5 5
Part 1 Indian Polity and Constitution 5 5
Part 1 Geography of India and the World 5 5
Part 1 Indian Economy and Social Development 5 5
Part 1 Rural Society and Development 5 5
Part 1 Current Events of National and International Importance 5 5
Part 1 Science and Technology 5 5
Part 1 Environmental Ecology and Disaster Management 10 10
Part 1 Data Interpretation 10 10
Part 1 General Hindi 10 10
Part 2 Computer and Information Technology 15 15
Part 3 General Information Related to Uttar Pradesh 20 20
Total   100 100

In recent exams the paper has been given on an OMR sheet with pen. Your admit card will tell you the exact mode.

What this table is telling you

  • Part 1 has 65 marks, but they are broken into ten small subjects, so no single subject can carry you
  • Uttar Pradesh GK (20 marks) and Computer (15 marks) together are worth 35 marks, which is more than a third of the paper
  • Data Interpretation and General Hindi are 10 marks each, and both are scoring if you practise
  • Environment and Disaster Management has 10 marks, the same as Hindi, and is often skipped by students for no good reason

Negative marking, with numbers

For every wrong answer, one-fourth of the marks of that question is cut. Since each question is 1 mark, a wrong answer costs 0.25. Four wrong answers wipe out one correct answer. Unattempted questions carry no deduction, so a blind guess is not free. Guess only when you can remove at least two options.

Syllabus, part by part

Part 1: General knowledge and aptitude

  • History of India and Indian National Movement: social, cultural, economic and political side of Indian history, and the freedom movement with the rise of nationalism
  • Indian Polity and Constitution: constitutional development, the Constitution, political system and governance, Panchayati Raj, local self-government and public policy
  • Geography of India and the World: physical, social and economic geography, agriculture, horticulture, forestry, animal husbandry, population, urbanisation, smart cities and smart villages, plus general world geography
  • Indian Economy and Social Development: economic planning, NITI Aayog, Sustainable Development Goals, budget and financial system, agriculture, industry and trade, land reforms, effects of globalisation, and infrastructure like power, ports, roads, airports and railways
  • Rural Society and Development: rural development programmes and schemes, rural health, rural social development, land reforms, and central and state schemes related to the village
  • Current Events: important national and international events
  • Science and Technology: science and technology policy in daily life, achievements of Indians, space, defence, energy, nanotechnology, biotechnology, and issues of intellectual property and digital rights
  • Environmental Ecology and Disaster Management: ecosystem, wildlife, biodiversity, pollution, environmental impact assessment, climate change, the Disaster Management Act 2005, NDMA, SDMA, NDRF and SDRF
  • Data Interpretation: reading tables, graphs and diagrams, and drawing conclusions from statistical data

Part 1: General Hindi

  • Letters, office orders, notifications and circulars
  • Pronunciation, writing, vowels, consonants and matras
  • Sandhi and sandhi-viched, samas, prefixes and suffixes
  • Tatsam, ardhatatsam, tadbhav, deshaj and foreign words, and the parts of speech
  • Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, homonyms, similar words and the right word choice
  • Gender, number, person, tense, mood, aspect and voice
  • Types of sentences, sentence purity and punctuation
  • Idioms and proverbs

Part 2: Computer and Information Technology

  • Computer basics, hardware and software
  • Operating systems and common computer applications
  • Internet, email and digital communication
  • Word processing and spreadsheet applications
  • Networking, digital platforms and information technology
  • Cyber security, digital awareness and new technological developments

Part 3: General information about Uttar Pradesh

  • History, culture, art, architecture, festivals, folk dances, literature and regional languages
  • Geography, rivers, climate, soil, forests, wildlife, mines and minerals
  • Economy, agriculture, industry, business and employment
  • Polity, administration and state government schemes
  • Tourism, monuments and important places
  • Current events and recent achievements of the state

The detailed syllabus is attached with the official notice, so download it once and tick off topics as you finish them.

Salary

The posts under this exam have come under Level 2 and Level 3 of the 7th Pay Commission.

Pay level Pay scale
Level 2 ₹19,900 to ₹63,200
Level 3 ₹21,700 to ₹69,100

The exact pay depends on the post, so look at the pay column of the post you choose in the notice. Allowances like DA and HRA are added to the basic pay as per the state government rates. Some posts are permanent and some are temporary, and the notice marks which is which, so check this before you select a post.

How to prepare: start from the marks, not from the books

With a 100 mark paper broken into twelve subjects, the smartest way is to decide your study time by marks and by how easy each subject is to score.

Subject Marks How to approach it
General Information of Uttar Pradesh 20 Give this the most time. Read UP history, culture, rivers, districts, schemes and monuments, and make short notes for revision
Computer and IT 15 Learn basics, shortcut keys, MS Word and Excel, internet and cyber security. Most questions are direct
General Hindi 10 Revise grammar rules and word lists. Solve questions on sandhi, samas, synonyms and idioms daily
Data Interpretation 10 Practise tables, bar graphs and pie charts with a timer. Speed matters more than formulas here
Environment and Disaster Management 10 Cover pollution, biodiversity, climate change and the disaster management bodies. A few days of focused study can give most of these marks
History, Polity, Geography, Economy, Rural Development, Science, Current Events 35 Use NCERT books of Class 6 to 12 for basics. Add rural development schemes and keep a notebook for current affairs

A simple 90 day plan

  1. Days 1 to 30: finish the basics of every subject once. Do not go deep yet. The aim is to see the whole syllabus.
  2. Days 31 to 60: go subject by subject with practice questions. Spend extra time on UP GK, Computer, Hindi and Data Interpretation.
  3. Days 61 to 90: take full length mocks of 100 questions in 2 hours, check every mistake and revise your short notes.

Do not forget PET. Its normalised score decides whether you are shortlisted, so a candidate who is also preparing for the next PET should not leave that preparation behind.

Handling the paper on exam day

Start with the parts you are most sure about, such as Hindi and Computer, and collect the safe marks first. Keep Data Interpretation for a calm stretch since it takes longer. Because of the 0.25 cut, mark an answer only when you are fairly confident. Keep the last ten minutes for checking the OMR sheet, since wrong bubbling is a loss that has nothing to do with knowledge.

Mistakes that quietly cost marks

  • Skipping UP GK because it feels like too much to remember, when it carries the highest marks of any single subject
  • Treating Computer as an easy 15 and not revising it even once
  • Choosing a post without reading its extra condition, like CCC or experience
  • Mismatch between the date of birth, name or category in the form and the documents
  • Applying under a reserved category without a valid certificate, or as a non-UP resident
  • Guessing too many questions and losing marks to negative marking
  • Not practising the OMR sheet before the exam

UPSSSC Combined Lower Subordinate Services (10+2) Vacancy & Application Dates

Questions people ask

Is PET compulsory for this exam?

Yes. You must have appeared in the PET and have a valid score. Shortlisting for the main exam is done on the normalised PET score, and candidates with a zero or negative score are not shortlisted.

Can graduates apply for the 10+2 level posts?

12th pass is the minimum qualification, so graduates can usually apply too. Check the notice for the exact rule and for any extra condition of the post.

Is there an interview?

No. The main written exam decides the merit, and it is followed by document verification.

How many questions come in the main exam?

There are 100 objective questions for 100 marks, and the time given is 2 hours.

Is there negative marking?

Yes. One-fourth of the marks of the question is cut for each wrong answer. For a 1 mark question this is 0.25.

Which subject has the most marks?

General Information of Uttar Pradesh has 20 marks, which is the highest for any single subject. Computer comes next with 15 marks.

Is the syllabus the same for 10+2 and graduate level?

No. Both levels have separate notices and the pattern is not the same. For example, the 10+2 level paper has smaller sections for History, Geography, Polity and Economy, while the graduate level has different weight for some subjects. Always follow the syllabus of the level you are applying for.

What is the age limit?

In recent notices it has been 18 to 40 years for most posts, with a tighter range of 21 to 30 years for posts that need experience. Relaxation is given as per UP government rules.

Do I need to be a resident of Uttar Pradesh?

Reservation benefits are for permanent residents of Uttar Pradesh only. Candidates from other states are treated as Unreserved, as per recent notices.

Do I need CCC or any computer certificate?

Only for some posts. In recent notices, the Gram Panchayat Officer post has asked for a CCC certificate from NIELIT. Most other posts have not, but the Computer part of the paper is there for everyone.

How long does preparation take?

If you start from the basics, around three months of steady daily study is a fair target. If you are also preparing for PET at the same time, plan for more.

contents.content:
RRB NTPC 12th level is one of the biggest railway exams for candidates who have passed Class 12. It is held by the Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) to select clerks and ticket staff for Indian Railways. The exam is fully computer based, there is no interview, and the qualification needed is only Class 12. That is why lakhs of candidates fill the form every time it comes.

The questions are not very tough, but the competition is. Marks are decided by speed, basic concepts and regular practice. This guide explains the whole exam in one place: who can give it, how selection works, the paper pattern, the syllabus, cut off, salary and a practical way to prepare.

The details here follow the pattern used in recent RRB NTPC 12th level notices. Age limit, fee, vacancies and small rules can change from one notice to the next, so always match the key points with the latest official notification at rrb.indianrailways.gov.in before applying.

About the exam

NTPC means Non-Technical Popular Categories. These are office and station jobs that do not need a technical degree or diploma. Railways hold the NTPC exam at two levels. The graduate level is for posts like Station Master and Goods Guard, and the 12th level (also called Undergraduate or UG) is for the clerk side posts. This guide is only about the 12th level.

Point Details
Conducted by Railway Recruitment Boards (RRB)
Exam level 12th (+2 stage), Undergraduate
Exam mode Computer based test (CBT), online
Papers 2 (CBT 1 and CBT 2)
Subjects General Awareness, Mathematics, General Intelligence and Reasoning
Question type Multiple choice, one correct answer
Negative marking 1/3 mark for every wrong answer
Interview No

Posts under the 12th level exam

In recent notices, the exam has been held for these four posts.

Post Department Pay level
Commercial cum Ticket Clerk Commercial Level 3
Junior Clerk cum Typist General Level 2
Accounts Clerk cum Typist Accounts Level 2
Trains Clerk Operating Level 2

One common exam is held for all of them. The post you get depends on your merit rank and the choices you gave in the form.

Eligibility

Educational qualification

You should have passed Class 12 (+2 stage) or an equivalent exam from a recognised board. General category candidates need at least 50% marks in the aggregate. SC, ST, ex-servicemen and PwBD candidates are exempt from the 50% condition, and so are candidates who hold a higher qualification such as a graduation degree.

Graduates and post-graduates can also give this exam, because Class 12 is only the minimum. Candidates whose Class 12 result is still awaited are not eligible, as the qualification must be complete by the last date of the application.

Age limit

In recent notices the age limit has been 18 to 30 years, counted as on a cut off date given in the notice. The upper limit is relaxed for reserved categories.

Category Relaxation in upper age
SC / ST 5 years
OBC (non-creamy layer) 3 years
PwBD (UR / EWS) 10 years
PwBD (OBC NCL) 13 years
PwBD (SC / ST) 15 years
Ex-servicemen 3 years (UR / EWS), 6 years (OBC), 8 years (SC / ST), after deducting the service period
Age is counted on the date given in the notice, not on the day you fill the form. Check that date every time a new notice comes.

Medical standards

Every post has its own medical fitness standard, including eyesight. It is checked after you clear the written papers. It does not change your exam preparation, but read the standard of the post you want before you choose it in the form.

Application fee

The fee is paid online while filling the form. A major part of it is returned after you appear in CBT 1.

Category Fee Refund after appearing in CBT 1
General, OBC, EWS ₹500 ₹400
SC, ST, ex-servicemen, PwBD, female, transgender, minorities, EBC ₹250 ₹250

Bank charges are cut from the refund. EBC is a fee concession for candidates whose family income is below ₹50,000 a year, and it needs an income certificate or BPL card. It is not a reservation category.

Selection process

Selection has four stages, and you move ahead only after clearing the one before it.

  1. CBT 1: a screening test, common for all posts
  2. CBT 2: the main paper, which decides the merit
  3. Document verification: your certificates are checked against your form
  4. Medical examination: fitness test for the post

The marks of CBT 1 are not added to the final score. You only have to clear its cut off. The final merit list is made from CBT 2 marks, and document verification and medical are qualifying stages.

Earlier, the typist posts also had a typing skill test (30 words per minute in English or 25 in Hindi). In the latest notice this test has been removed for Junior Clerk cum Typist and Accounts Clerk cum Typist, so check the notice to see if it is held.

Do not treat CBT 1 as the real exam. It only opens the door to CBT 2, and your rank depends fully on CBT 2, which is of a higher level.

CBT 1 exam pattern

Subject Questions Marks
General Awareness 40 40
Mathematics 30 30
General Intelligence and Reasoning 30 30
Total 100 100
  • Time: 90 minutes (120 minutes for PwBD candidates with a scribe)
  • Each question carries 1 mark
  • 1/3 mark is cut for each wrong answer
  • Marks are used only for shortlisting, not for final merit

CBT 2 exam pattern

Subject Questions Marks
General Awareness 50 50
Mathematics 35 35
General Intelligence and Reasoning 35 35
Total 120 120
  • Time: 90 minutes (120 minutes for PwBD candidates with a scribe)
  • Each question carries 1 mark
  • 1/3 mark is cut for each wrong answer
  • Final merit is made from this paper

General Awareness carries the most marks in both papers, so it can make or break your score. Maths and Reasoning together decide the rest, and both can be scored well with steady practice.

How the marking works

For a 1 mark question, a wrong answer costs 1/3 mark, which is about 0.33. So if you get 3 answers wrong, you lose 1 full mark. Unattempted questions carry no deduction. Because of this, every blind guess is a small risk, and you should guess only when you can remove at least two options.

Languages and shifts

The paper is given in Hindi, English and many regional languages, and you pick your language while filling the form. When the exam is held in more than one shift, the board normalises the marks across shifts so that no one gets an advantage from an easy or tough shift. Check the notice for the exact list of languages and the rule that is followed.

Syllabus in detail

The syllabus is the same for CBT 1 and CBT 2. What changes is the number of questions and the difficulty. Maths is mostly of school level, and reasoning is about speed and logic.

Mathematics

Area Topics to cover
Number work Number system, simplification, fractions, decimals, LCM and HCF
Ratio and percentage Ratio and proportion, percentage, average
Money problems Profit and loss, discount, simple interest, compound interest
Time and motion Time and work, time and distance
Geometry and algebra Mensuration, basic algebra, geometry, trigonometry basics

General Intelligence and Reasoning

Area Topics to cover
Series and coding Number series, alphabet series, coding-decoding
Logic Syllogism, statement and conclusions, Venn diagrams
Relations Blood relations, analogy, classification
Puzzles and operations Puzzles, mathematical operations

General Awareness

Area Topics to cover
Current affairs National and international events, sports, awards, government schemes
Static GK Important places, books and authors, important days, firsts in India
History and geography Ancient, medieval and modern India, physical features, rivers, climate
Polity and economy Basics of the Constitution, banking, budget, common economic terms
General science Basic physics, chemistry and biology

Cut off and merit

There are two kinds of cut off in this exam. The first is the CBT 1 cut off, which decides who gets to write CBT 2. The second is the final merit in CBT 2, which decides who gets which post. Cut offs are different for each category and each RRB, and they change every year with the number of vacancies, the number of candidates and the difficulty of the paper.

So do not depend on the previous year’s cut off alone. Aim to score well above it in your mocks, because that gives you a safe gap.

Document verification and medical

Candidates who make the merit list are called for document verification. You have to show the originals of the certificates you used in the form, like Class 10 and Class 12 marksheets, category certificate, EBC certificate if you claimed it, a photo ID and passport size photos. Any mismatch between the form and the documents can cancel your candidature.

After this comes the medical examination for the post. Only those who pass it are finally selected.

Salary and benefits

These posts come under the 7th Pay Commission.

Post Pay level Starting basic pay
Commercial cum Ticket Clerk Level 3 ₹21,700
Junior Clerk cum Typist Level 2 ₹19,900
Accounts Clerk cum Typist Level 2 ₹19,900
Trains Clerk Level 2 ₹19,900

Basic pay is only one part of the salary. DA, HRA, transport allowance and other allowances come on top, and they depend on the rates in force and the city of posting. So your in-hand salary is higher than the basic pay. Railway staff also get medical facilities, leave, pension related benefits and travel passes.

How to prepare

Subject wise plan

Subject CBT 2 marks How to prepare
General Awareness 50 Read NCERT books of Class 6 to 10 for history, geography and science. Follow current affairs daily and revise them every week
Mathematics 35 Learn tables, squares, cubes and basic formulas first. Then practise topic wise with a timer and go back to your wrong answers
Reasoning 35 Solve a few questions every day. Start with series, coding-decoding and relations, and take up puzzles later

Step by step

  1. Read the syllabus and solve two or three previous year papers to understand the level of questions.
  2. Spend the first month on basics: maths formulas, NCERT reading and easy reasoning.
  3. Next, practise topic wise questions every day and note your mistakes in a copy.
  4. Start current affairs early and revise them every week, not only before the exam.
  5. In the last phase, give full length mocks of both CBT 1 and CBT 2 pattern and revise your notes.

Time and attempt strategy

Start with the subject you are strongest in, so you collect safe marks first. Keep General Awareness for a calm moment, because it is quick when you know the answer and wastes time when you do not. Do not stay on one tough question for more than a minute. Skip it and come back if time is left. Practise finishing a full paper in 90 minutes, with a few minutes kept for review.

Many candidates know the answers but run out of time because they never practised with a timer. Take at least 15 to 20 full mocks before the exam.

Exam day tips

  • Reach the centre early, with your admit card and a valid photo ID
  • Read each question fully before you pick an option
  • Use the on-screen calculator rule given in the instructions, and do rough work on the sheet provided
  • Keep the last few minutes to go through the questions you marked for review

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Preparing only for CBT 1 level and getting stuck in CBT 2
  • Reading too many books instead of revising one properly
  • Never checking the mistakes after a mock test
  • Leaving current affairs for the last month
  • Attempting every question and losing marks to negative marking
  • Form mistakes like a wrong category, wrong RRB choice or mismatched documents

Common questions

How many papers are there in RRB NTPC 12th level?

There are two computer based papers, CBT 1 and CBT 2. CBT 1 is for screening and CBT 2 decides the final merit.

Do CBT 1 marks count in the final merit?

No. You only need to clear the CBT 1 cut off. The final merit is made from CBT 2.

Is there negative marking?

Yes. 1/3 mark is cut for every wrong answer in both papers.

Can graduates give the 12th level exam?

Yes. Class 12 is the minimum qualification, so graduates can also apply if they fit the age limit.

Is there a typing test?

In the latest notice it has been removed for the typist posts, though earlier cycles had it. Check the notice to confirm.

Is there an interview?

No. Selection depends on CBT 1, CBT 2, document verification and medical examination.

What is the difference between NTPC graduate and 12th level?

The graduate level needs a degree and covers posts like Station Master and Goods Guard. The 12th level needs Class 12 and covers the clerk side posts. Both have separate notices and separate pay levels.

Can I apply to more than one RRB?

No. You can apply to only one RRB in a notice, so choose carefully.

Which subject is the most important?

General Awareness has the most marks (40 in CBT 1 and 50 in CBT 2), but all three subjects count, so do not leave any one behind.

How long does preparation take?

If your basics are fine, four to six months of regular daily study is a fair target. If you are starting from zero, plan for more time.

What is the age limit?

In recent notices it has been 18 to 30 years, with 5 years relaxation for SC and ST and 3 years for OBC (non-creamy layer). The cut off date for counting age is given in each notice.

Does the exam come every year?

The railway board brings the notice on its own schedule, and the gap can change. So do not wait for the notice to start. People who begin only after it is out usually find the time short.

contents.content:
The WBPSC Clerkship exam is one of the most popular government job exams in West Bengal, mainly because you only need to be Madhyamik (10th) pass to apply. The West Bengal Public Service Commission (WBPSC) holds it to fill Lower Division Clerk and Lower Division Assistant posts, along with other similar clerical posts, in the Secretariat, Directorates, District Offices and Regional Offices of the state government.

Because the qualification is basic, lakhs of candidates apply every time. That means the exam is not hard in terms of difficulty level, but it is tough in terms of competition. This guide covers everything in one place: who can apply, how many stages there are, the full exam pattern, the syllabus, the salary, and how to prepare from scratch.

Looking for study material? This guide also includes free WBPSC Clerkship PDF books in English and Bangla: an English syllabus book and MCQ banks for English, Arithmetic and General Studies. Jump to the free PDF downloads.

Everything below is based on the pattern followed in recent WBPSC Clerkship notifications. Details like age limit, fee, qualifying marks and vacancy numbers can change from one notification to the next, so always confirm them in the latest official notification at psc.wb.gov.in before you apply.

The exam at a glance

Point Details
Conducting body West Bengal Public Service Commission (WBPSC)
Posts Lower Division Clerk, Lower Division Assistant and equivalent clerical posts
Minimum qualification Madhyamik (Class 10) pass or equivalent
Age limit 18 to 40 years for general candidates, with relaxation for reserved categories
Selection stages Part I (objective), Part II (written), computer knowledge and typing test
Pay scale Pay Level 6, roughly ₹22,700 to ₹58,500 plus allowances
Job location Within West Bengal
Application mode Online through the official WBPSC website

Eligibility

Educational qualification

You need to have passed the Madhyamik examination of the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education, or an equivalent examination. Higher qualifications like Higher Secondary, graduation or post-graduation are also accepted, since the rule is a minimum. The notification may also mention basic computer knowledge as a requirement, so read that part carefully.

Age limit

In recent notifications, the minimum age is 18 years. The maximum age depends on your category, and it is counted as on a cut-off date mentioned in the notification, not on the day you apply.

Category Minimum age Maximum age (as in recent notifications)
General, and SC/ST/OBC candidates of other states 18 years 40 years
OBC (non-creamy layer) 18 years 43 years
SC/ST of West Bengal, persons with disabilities (PwBD) 18 years 45 years

Other relaxations, such as for ex-servicemen and government employees, are given as per state rules. The notification lists all of them.

Other conditions

You must meet the citizenship, character and medical conditions stated in the notification. You will also need valid documents, like your Madhyamik certificate, caste certificate if applicable, a recent photograph and a signature, at the time of applying and later at document verification.

How many exams are there? The three stages

Many beginners ask how many exams they have to give. The Clerkship selection has three stages, and you have to clear them one after another.

  1. Part I: an objective-type test with multiple choice questions
  2. Part II: a conventional written test in English and a language of your choice
  3. Computer knowledge and typing test: a practical test for those who qualify in both written parts

The final merit list is made from the combined marks of Part I and Part II. The typing test is a qualifying stage, which means you have to pass it, but its marks do not add to your merit score.

Part I: exam pattern

Subject Questions Marks
English 30 30
Arithmetic 30 30
General Studies 40 40
Total 100 100
  • Duration is 90 minutes for the whole paper
  • Each question carries 1 mark
  • Every wrong answer costs 0.25 marks
  • Questions are asked in English and Bengali
  • The paper has multiple choice questions with one correct answer

General Studies carries the most marks, so it has the biggest effect on your Part I score. Arithmetic and English together make up the other 60 marks, and both can be scored well with steady practice.

Part II: exam pattern

Group Subject Marks
Group A English 50
Group B Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali (your choice) 50
Total   100 marks in 60 minutes

This is a descriptive paper, so you write your answers by hand, and there is no negative marking. It tests basic writing skills, not literature or deep grammar. The next section explains what is asked in each group.

Computer knowledge and typing test

Candidates who qualify in Part I and Part II are called for a test on elementary computer operation and typing. The typing speeds prescribed in recent notifications are 20 words per minute in English and 10 words per minute in Bengali. This test is qualifying in nature. It is not hard, but plenty of candidates fail it by ignoring it until the last moment, so start practising typing early. You can build your speed with our free typing practice tool.

Qualifying marks

You must score a minimum percentage on the combined marks of Part I and Part II to qualify. Recent notifications set it like this.

Category Qualifying marks
Unreserved (General) 40%
EWS 40%
OBC 38%
SC 35%
ST 30%
PwBD 30%
Ex-servicemen 30%
Meritorious sports persons 40%

Qualifying only gets you into the merit list. Your actual rank depends on how many marks you score compared with other candidates, and cut-offs vary from cycle to cycle depending on the difficulty of the paper and the number of vacancies.

Syllabus in detail

The paper is set at the Madhyamik standard. That means you don't need advanced books. If your Class 9 and 10 basics are strong, you already have a head start.

Part I: English (30 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Vocabulary Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, spelling
Grammar Tenses, articles, prepositions, subject-verb agreement, voice, narration, modals
Sentence work Sentence structure, error spotting, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks

Part I: Arithmetic (30 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Number work Divisibility, fractions, decimals, simplification, LCM and HCF
Ratio and percentage Ratio and proportion, percentage, average, partnership
Money problems Simple interest, profit and loss
Time and motion Time and distance, time and work
Basic geometry Area of rectangles and squares, and simple shapes

Part I: General Studies (40 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Indian history Broad understanding of ancient, medieval and modern India, with the freedom movement
Indian geography Physical features, rivers, climate, resources and agriculture of India
Current events Important national events, with special reference to India, and major world events
Everyday science Basic physics, chemistry and biology, health and daily life science

Questions on West Bengal appear in many state-level exams, so keep a light layer of West Bengal general knowledge on top of this, such as important places, rivers, personalities and recent state news.

Part II: Group A, English (50 marks)

  • Drafting a report in English from the information given
  • Precis writing, which means shortening a passage while keeping its main points
  • Translation from Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali into English

Part II: Group B, your chosen language (50 marks)

  • Drafting a report in the chosen language
  • Precis writing in the chosen language
  • Translation from English into the chosen language
The exact tasks in Part II can be worded a little differently in each notification. Check the syllabus section of the latest advertisement for the final list.

Salary and benefits

Clerks in West Bengal are placed at Pay Level 6 of the state pay structure, with a scale of roughly ₹22,700 to ₹58,500. The starting basic pay is at the lower end of that range, and it grows with annual increments and promotions.

On top of basic pay you get Dearness Allowance, House Rent Allowance, medical benefits and other admissible allowances. DA and HRA rates are decided by the state government and can change, so your in-hand salary depends on the rates in force at the time and the city where you are posted. Deductions like contributions towards pension or provident fund and professional tax come off before you receive it.

The pay is modest at the start, but the job comes with security, regular increments, leave and pension-related benefits, and a clear promotion path. That is why so many people prefer it over uncertain private jobs.

The job and career growth

As a clerk, your work is mostly office work: handling files and notes, maintaining records, drafting letters, entering data on computers, dealing with public queries at a counter in some offices, and helping senior officers with day-to-day paperwork. Postings are within West Bengal, in the Secretariat in Kolkata, directorates, or district and regional offices.

Promotions generally move from clerk to higher clerical and assistant posts and then to supervisory posts, through seniority and departmental exams. The speed varies by department, so treat your starting post as one you will hold for a good while. Vacancies are sometimes announced after the application stage, and appointments may start on a temporary basis under the rules of the notification.

How to prepare for the Clerkship exam

Since the level is Madhyamik, your preparation should be built on basics and speed, not on heavy books. Here is a simple way to split your time.

Subject Marks How to prepare
General Studies 40 Read school textbooks of Class 6 to 10 for history, geography and science. Read a newspaper daily and keep short notes on current events
Arithmetic 30 Learn tables, squares and basic formulas first. Then practise topic by topic with a timer, and revisit mistakes
English 30 Study grammar rules from a simple book, build vocabulary daily, and solve error spotting and fill-in-the-blank sets
Part II writing 100 Write one short report, precis and translation each week from the start, in both English and your chosen language
Typing Qualifying Practise English and Bengali typing for 20 to 30 minutes a day, since the required speed is low but needs practice

A simple study order

  1. Start with the syllabus and a few previous year papers to see the level of questions
  2. Spend the first month on basics: arithmetic fundamentals, grammar and school textbook reading
  3. In the next phase, practise topic-wise questions every day (the free WBPSC Clerkship MCQ PDFs below are made for this) and keep a notebook of mistakes
  4. Start Part II writing early, because handwriting speed and clear drafting take months to build
  5. In the last phase, take full-length Part I mocks and revise your notes
  6. Do not leave typing practice for the end

Part I strategy that works

With 0.25 negative marking, blind guessing hurts. If you can remove two options with confidence, a guess is usually fine. If you have no idea, skip it. Do the sections you are strongest in first, and keep General Studies for a calm moment, since it is quick if you know the topic and a waste of time if you don't. Practise finishing a full paper in 90 minutes, with a few minutes left to review.

Part II strategy that works

For the report and the precis, plain sentences are enough. Nobody is checking for fancy words. Have a clear start and finish, and keep to the word limit. In translation, get the meaning across correctly instead of converting every word one by one, because that usually gives you awkward sentences. And keep an eye on the clock while you practise. Sixty minutes for two languages disappears fast, and it is easy to run out of time on the second group.

Where people usually slip

The biggest slip is taking the exam lightly because the level is Madhyamik. The questions are simple, but lakhs of people are solving the same simple questions, and a few marks decide the rank. Part II comes next. Many people wait for the Part I result and only then start writing, and by that time there is hardly any room to fix their handwriting speed or their drafting.

Typing gets ignored too, since it feels like a formality. It isn't one. It is a qualifying stage, and you can't be selected without clearing it. A few smaller things also cost marks: reading five books instead of revising one properly, never looking at the mistakes in your mock tests, guessing too much in Part I, and getting documents or details wrong during the application and verification.

Common questions

Can graduates apply for the Clerkship exam?

Yes. Madhyamik is only the minimum, so graduates and post-graduates can apply too. They just have to fit the age limit and the other conditions in the notification.

Is there an interview?

Not in the process described in recent notifications. Your selection depends on the Part I and Part II marks, and after that you have to clear the computer and typing test.

Do I have to know Bengali?

Not for Part II, because you can pick Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali instead. The typing test is different, since it has a Bengali typing requirement. Check how the notification words it for your case.

Does the exam come every year?

No, there is no fixed yearly schedule. The gap between two notifications can be long, and nobody outside the commission knows the date beforehand. So don't wait for the advertisement to start. People who begin only after it comes out usually find the time too short.

How long does preparation take?

If your basics are decent, four to six months of regular daily study is a reasonable target. If you have been out of studies for years, or you are starting from nothing, plan for more.

Is there negative marking in Part II?

No. The 0.25 deduction is only for wrong answers in the objective Part I.

Where can I download WBPSC Clerkship PDF books for free?

You can download them from the free PDF section on this page. It has an English syllabus book and MCQ banks for English, Arithmetic and General Studies. No login is needed.

Is the WBPSC Clerkship PDF available in Bangla?

Yes. The Arithmetic MCQ Bank (পাটিগণিত) and the General Studies MCQ Bank (সাধারণ জ্ঞান) are available in Bangla, with answers and short explanations in Bangla. The English syllabus book and the English MCQ bank are in English.

Which book is best for WBPSC Clerkship?

No single book covers everything. Since the paper is at Madhyamik level, start with school textbooks of Class 6 to 10, use a syllabus book for English grammar, and practise MCQ banks for English, Arithmetic and General Studies with a timer. Then revise your mistakes before taking full-length mocks.

Final word

The WBPSC Clerkship exam rewards people who prepare the basics well and stay consistent. The syllabus is at the Madhyamik level, the pattern is simple, and the three stages are easy to understand. What separates those who get selected from those who don't is mostly practice: timed arithmetic sets, regular writing for Part II, a daily newspaper habit, and a bit of typing every day. Start with the official syllabus, use the free PDF books for practice, make a simple plan, and keep checking the official site for the latest notification.
